title: Chapter 132 — The Symphony
paragraphs: It was a clear, steel-blue day. In that all-pervading blue, the firmaments of air and sea could hardly be told apart; except that the thoughtful air was transparently pure and soft, with a woman's look, while the strong, manlike sea heaved with long, powerful, lingering swells, like Samson's chest as he sleeps.

High overhead, the snow-white wings of small, unspeckled birds glided this way and that; these were the gentle thoughts of the feminine air. But far down in the bottomless blue, mighty leviathans, swordfish and sharks rushed back and forth through the depths; and these were the strong, troubled, murderous thinkings of the masculine sea.
But though the two contrasted so within, without, the contrast was only in shades and shadows; those two seemed one — it was only the sex, as it were, that distinguished them.

High above, like a royal czar and king, the sun seemed to be giving this gentle air in marriage to this bold, rolling sea, as a bride is given to a groom. And at the encircling line of the horizon, a soft, trembling motion — seen most of all here at the equator — showed the fond, throbbing trust and the loving fears with which the poor bride gave away her bosom.

Bound up and twisted, gnarled and knotted with wrinkles, haggardly firm and unyielding, his eyes glowing like coals that still glow in the ashes of ruin, Ahab stood forth without tottering in the clear morning, lifting the splintered helmet of his brow to heaven's fair, girlish forehead.

Oh, immortal infancy and innocence of the azure! Invisible winged creatures that frolic all around us! Sweet childhood of air and sky! How oblivious you were of old Ahab's close-coiled woe! But just so have I seen little Miriam and Martha, laughing-eyed elves, heedlessly frolicking around their old father, playing with the circle of singed locks that grew on the edge of that burnt-out crater of his brain.

Crossing the deck slowly from the scuttle, Ahab leaned over the side and watched how his shadow in the water sank deeper and deeper before his eyes the harder he tried to see into the depths. But the lovely fragrances of that enchanted air did at last seem to drive away, for a moment, the cankerous thing in his soul. That glad, happy air, that winning sky, did at last stroke and caress him; the stepmother world, so long cruel — forbidding — now threw loving arms around his stubborn neck, and seemed to sob over him with joy, as if over someone whom, however willful and wayward, she could still find it in her heart to save and to bless. From under his slouched hat Ahab dropped a tear into the sea; and the whole Pacific held no wealth to match that one tiny drop.

Starbuck saw the old man — saw how heavily he leaned over the side; and in his own true heart he seemed to hear the boundless sobbing that crept out from the center of the calm all around. Taking care not to touch him or be noticed by him, he nevertheless came close to him and stood there.

"Oh, Starbuck! It is a mild, mild wind, and a mild-looking sky. On such a day — very much such a sweetness as this — I struck my first whale — a boy-harpooner of eighteen! Forty — forty — forty years ago! — ago! Forty years of continual whaling! Forty years of privation, and peril, and storm-time! Forty years on the pitiless sea! For forty years Ahab has forsaken the peaceful land, for forty years to make war on the horrors of the deep! Aye and yes, Starbuck, out of those forty years I have not spent three ashore. When I think of this life I have led — the desolation of solitude it has been; the masoned, walled town of a captain's exclusiveness, which lets in so little sympathy from the green country outside — oh, weariness! heaviness! Guinea-coast slavery of solitary command! — when I think of all this, only half-suspected, not so keenly known to me before — and how for forty years I have fed on dry salted fare, fit emblem of the dry nourishment of my soil! — while the poorest landsman has had fresh fruit to his daily hand, and broken the world's fresh bread against my moldy crusts — away, whole oceans away, from that young girl-wife I married when I was past fifty, and sailed for Cape Horn the next day, leaving only one dent in my marriage pillow — wife? wife? — rather a widow with her husband alive! Aye, I widowed that poor girl when I married her, Starbuck; and then the madness, the frenzy, the boiling blood and the smoking brow with which, for a thousand lowerings, old Ahab has furiously, foamingly chased his prey — more a demon than a man! — aye, aye! what a forty years' fool — fool — old fool, old Ahab has been! Why this strife of the chase? Why weary and palsy the arm at the oar, and the iron, and the lance? How is Ahab the richer or better now? Look. Oh, Starbuck! is it not hard that, with this weary load I bear, one poor leg should have been snatched from under me? Here, brush this old hair aside; it blinds me, so that I seem to weep. Locks so gray never grew except out of some ashes! But do I look very old, so very, very old, Starbuck? I feel deadly faint, bowed and humped, as though I were Adam, staggering beneath the piled-up centuries since Paradise. God! God! God! — crack my heart! — stave in my brain! — mockery! mockery! bitter, biting mockery of gray hairs, have I lived enough joy to wear you, and to seem and feel so intolerably old? Close! stand close to me, Starbuck; let me look into a human eye; it is better than to gaze into sea or sky; better than to gaze upon God. By the green land; by the bright hearth-stone! this is the magic glass, man; I see my wife and my child in your eye. No, no; stay on board, on board! — do not lower when I do, when branded Ahab gives chase to Moby Dick. That hazard shall not be yours. No, no! not with the far-away home I see in that eye!"

"Oh, my Captain! my Captain! noble soul! grand old heart, after all! Why should anyone give chase to that hated fish? Away with me! Let us fly these deadly waters! Let us go home! Wife and child, too, are Starbuck's — wife and child of his brotherly, sisterly, play-fellow youth; just as yours, sir, are the wife and child of your loving, longing, paternal old age! Away! Let us away! — let me alter the course this instant! How cheerily, how hilariously, O my Captain, we would bowl along on our way to see old Nantucket again! I think, sir, they have some such mild blue days, just like this one, in Nantucket."

"They have, they have. I have seen them — on some summer days, in the morning. About this time — yes, he's having his noon nap now — the boy wakes up full of life and sits up in bed, and his mother tells him about me, about cannibal old me; how I'm away out on the deep, but will still come back to dance him again."

"It's my Mary, my Mary herself! She promised that every morning my boy would be carried up the hill to catch the first glimpse of his father's sail! Yes, yes! No more! It's settled! We head for Nantucket! Come, my Captain, work out the course, and let's be off! Look, look! The boy's face at the window! The boy's hand on the hill!"
But Ahab looked away; he shook like a blighted fruit tree and dropped his last, charred apple to the ground.

"What is it, what nameless, inscrutable, unearthly thing is it; what deceitful, hidden lord and master, what cruel, remorseless emperor commands me, so that against all natural loves and longings I keep pushing and crowding and jamming myself on all the time, recklessly making myself ready to do what in my own proper, natural heart I would not dare so much as to dare? Is Ahab, Ahab? Is it I, God, or who, that lifts this arm? But if the great sun does not move by himself, but is like an errand-boy in heaven; and if not one single star can revolve except by some invisible power; how then can this one small heart beat, this one small brain think thoughts, unless God does that beating, does that thinking, does that living, and not I? By heaven, man, we are turned round and round in this world like that windlass over there, and Fate is the handspike. And all the while, look! that smiling sky, and this unsounded sea! Look! See that albacore there! Who put it into him to chase that flying-fish and sink his fangs in it? Where do murderers go, man? Who is to pass sentence, when the judge himself is dragged before the bar? But it is a mild, mild wind, and a mild-looking sky; and the air smells now as if it blew from a faraway meadow; they have been making hay somewhere under the slopes of the Andes, Starbuck, and the mowers are sleeping in the new-mown hay. Sleeping? Aye, however hard we toil, we all sleep in the field at last. Sleep? Aye, and rust amid the green, like last year's scythes thrown down and left in the half-cut rows — Starbuck!"
But blanched to a corpse's hue with despair, the mate had stolen away.
Ahab crossed the deck to look over the other side, but started at the sight of two fixed eyes reflected in the water there. Fedallah was leaning, motionless, over the same rail.
